Shanghai Jiao Tong University, China (Fu, Zhang B., Guan, Liu W., Zhang W., Yu; first three as interns at Meituan); Meituan, China (Zhu, Qiu, Cao, Cai)

Proposes an evaluation method; secondary: Compares — PRDBench (50 PRD-based Python projects built with an agent-driven annotation pipeline) and PRDJudge (fine-tuned Agent-as-a-Judge), used to compare 12 code agents (8 minimal ADK agents with different LLMs, 4 commercial CLI agents) in development and debug rounds

No SDD approach named. PRD-centred development setting: agents implement a project from a Product Requirement Document (PRD.md) and a criteria scheme (detailed_test_plan.json). Agents: Minimal agents (authors' Agent Development Kit agent, https://github.com/AGI-Eval-Official/Minimal-CodeAgent) and commercial Claude Code, CodeX, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code (versions not stated). Evaluator: PRDJudge (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, LoRA fine-tuned)

PRD.md (Requirement Overview, Functional Requirements, Data Requirements; mean 105.22 lines), generated by a code agent (e.g. Claude Code); criteria scheme detailed_test_plan.json with metrics structured as Arrange-Act-Assert (types: unit test, shell interaction, file comparison), test artefacts and input data; PRDJudge score report (reports/) as input to the debug round

Agent evaluation: Round 1 DEV (implement the whole project from PRD and test plan, no questions allowed), Round 2 DEBUG (fix deducted items from the PRDJudge report). Benchmark construction: 1 PRD and test plan initialization; 2 scaffold and criteria generation; 3 human inspection; 4 agent-based fix and refinement (at least 5 rounds); 5 remove scaffold

None during agent runs (autonomous). In benchmark construction: human inspection of criteria scheme vs scaffold and PRD, with feedback to the agent over at least 5 refinement rounds; human annotation of judge ground truth (two annotators plus arbitrator)
Specification format only: PRD plus test plan given as input to autonomous agents in a two-round develop/debug flow; no SDD workflow run
Not classifiable (no SDD approach; authors' wording: 'PRD-centered benchmark', 'The PRD serves as the evaluation blueprint')
New project: agents generate the code from scratch (scaffold removed)

50 Python projects in 20 domains; 1,258 evaluation metrics (408 unit test, 732 shell interaction, 118 file comparison); PRD mean 105.22 lines; scaffold size mean 2,583.8 lines (median 1,279; 188-9,185); generated code in Round 1 from about 1,700 to 6,233 lines on average per agent

Python projects across 20 domains (e.g. data analysis, artificial intelligence, automation, application development, algorithms, information security, education, computer networks, software engineering, game development); seeds from an internal AI product platform, CS course projects and theses

N/A (autonomous agents). None for agent use. Benchmark construction effort: about 8 hours per project for annotators

Judge quality: Human Alignment Rate (HAR, exact match with human scores) in-domain and out-of-domain; stability over three runs: Unanimous Agreement Rate (UAR) and Pairwise Agreement Rate (PAR); judge tool-use distribution; fixed-inference vs free-development scores (Fig. 7)

Automatic: PRDJudge executes each criterion (pytest, shell commands with simulated input, file comparison; GPT-4o via deal_graph for images) and writes a JSON report with score 0/1/2; logs for time, tokens and lines (CodeX logs unavailable). Manual: ground truth by two annotators with a third arbitrator (10% of agreed cases re-checked); in-domain test set 513 metrics, out-of-domain 605 metrics from 26 repositories. Settings: temperature 0.1, top-p 1.0, top-k 100

Success criterion per metric: PRDJudge score 2 = output strictly matches the criteria scheme; no criterion stated by the authors for a configuration, so quality and cost verdicts for every entry: no criterion stated by the authors. Tasks: 50 PRDBench projects (fixed-interface inference; free development as proof of concept). Configurations: 8 minimal ADK agents with different LLMs (to compare LLMs fairly) and 4 commercial CLI agents with their vendor models. Baseline: none formal. Held constant: prompts (Appendix E), PRD and test plan, Python virtual environment (pip allowed), sampling settings (temperature 0.1), judge (PRDJudge). Acceptance: criteria scheme executed by PRDJudge. Repetitions: Not stated for agent runs (single run implied); judge stability checked over 3 runs. Human intervention: none (agents told not to ask questions); debug round uses the judge report as feedback

DEV: best minimal Claude-4.5 69.19, then GPT-5.2 62.49 and CodeX 62.09; minimal agents generally above their commercial counterparts. DEBUG: best Claude Code 70.25, then GPT-5.2 69.00; commercial agents mostly improve (Claude Code +13.60, Gemini CLI +10.22, CodeX +2.97, but Qwen Code -3.96), strong minimal agents can regress (Claude-4.5 -12.79, DeepSeek-V3.2 -15.31). Unit-test failures hardest to fix. Judges: PRDJudge HAR 91.75 (in-domain) / 92.69 (out-of-domain) vs Claude-4.5 90.64/88.10, GPT-5.2 89.76/87.09, Qwen3-Coder-480B 90.32/87.91, base Qwen3-Coder-30B 70.52/55.46, humans 95.83; PRDJudge lowest time (107.85 s per metric) and highest stability (UAR 94.19, PAR 96.07). Free development: rankings stable, smaller variance. No significance tests

Distinguished agents (11.29 to 70.25 pass rate) and judges; judge stable across three runs, but agent runs not repeated. Limitations stated: free development mode introduces evaluation noise because the judge must adapt test interfaces, so fixed inference is recommended; ground-truth annotation required substantial human effort

No threats-to-validity section. Stated: free development evaluation is noisy (agent errors confounded with judge interface-rewriting failures); human ground truth is costly (one-time). Findings/gaps: foundation model sets the zero-shot ceiling; commercial frameworks constrain generation but help debugging; unconstrained models regress in long-context debugging; system-level (shell, file) interactions harder than unit tests. Future work: dynamic interface mapping in PRDJudge for unconstrained evaluation

Inconsistencies: Table 1 gives Claude Code 45.5% on PRDBench (p. 2) while Table 4 gives 56.65 (DEV) and 70.25 (DEBUG) (p. 8); CodeX Enhance +2.97 vs 65.02 - 62.09 = 2.93 (p. 8); Table 8 says CodeX logs are unavailable but lists a CodeX line count (p. 13); the pass-rate formula from 0/1/2 scores is not given; the conclusion says system-level interactions pose far greater challenges than unit tests (p. 9), while Section 5.4.3 says error rates are relatively uniform across the three test types and unit-test failures are the hardest to debug (p. 9); Section 5.4.1 and the conclusion say commercial agents 'excel in iterative debugging' (p. 8-9), while Appendix D says only Claude Code gains in the debug phase and the other commercial frameworks 'do not show significant debugging dividends' (p. 14); appendix prompt refers to 'Section 4.7' for free development, which is Section 5.4.4 (p. 14); model named Qwen3-Coder-480B-A3B (p. 6-7); case-study repositories named 'ADK_claude_3_7_1' and 'ADK_gpt_5_4' do not match the models evaluated (p. 11-12). Tables 4, 8 and Fig. 7 were read from garbled text extraction and should be checked against the PDF. Data: PRDBench at https://github.com/AGI-Eval-Official/PRDBench; PRDJudge weights at https://huggingface.co/AGI-Eval/PRDjudge; minimal agent code released (p. 2, 6). No pre-registration.
